newsitem.title: USA: Clinton team fends off attacks on river plan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton team fends off attacks on river plan.

text.p: Three top Clinton administration officials Tuesday attempted to defend a riverfront revival plan that some western lawmakers said would amount to another federal land grab.

Under the American Heritage Rivers initiative announced by President Clinton in his State of the Union address last February, 10 rivers nominated by local communities would be selected annually to receive federal help to restore historic riverfront areas.

The proposal, popular in many parts of the country, backfired when western property rights advocates flooded politicians with complaints that this was a new bid by federal bureaucrats to dictate land use and override states' rights.

"It seems every time I open the Federal Register, there is a new effort by the federal government to become the nanny of western resources," Representative Helen Chenoweth, an Idaho Republican, said at a contentious House Resources Committee hearing.

Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt, Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and Council on Environmental Quality Chairwoman Kathleen McGinty said the plan was only meant to cut red tape and channel federal resources more efficiently to communities.

"It is 100 percent voluntary ... this is 100 percent locally driven," McGinty said. "No new regulatory requirements or restrictions of any kind will come through this initiative. ... It is not an attempt to take anyone's private property."
"My fear is that this programme is nothing more than a thinly veiled attempt by the federal government to grab more power," said Utah Republican Representative Chris Cannon.

The committee questioned how the administration was going to fund the plan. Members said it would require their approval if agencies were planning to take money away from other programmes to pay salaries for officials that would be appointed to assist the selected communities.

Babbitt said no new people would be needed to carry out the plan, but an official would be named as the point of contact to help each community deal with federal agencies. "We can use existing funds," Glickman said.
While the officials said rivers would be selected based on community support, Republicans said the administration must make clear whose say in the community would be counted in evaluating requests.
McGinty tried to reassure them that if any local government opposed a designation, "that would be an extremely high hurdle for that particular application."
The administration expects to start receiving applications in September, after it has received public input on how the programme should be run.
